Photograph: NCJ Media Independent Office for Police Conduct Watchdog investigating after ‘multiple’ people die in crash between police vehicle and car in Yorkshire IOPC says police were pursuing a car before the collision on the A66 near Middlesbrough Geneva Abdul Sat 22 Aug 2026 08.23 EDT First published on Sat 22 Aug 2026 05.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The police regulator has launched an investigation after ‘multiple people’ died in a collision involving a police vehicle near Middlesbrough . A number of people died in the crash on the A66 in South Bank, North Yorkshire , in the early hours of Saturday morning, according to local authorities. “Around 3.39am this morning, a collision took place involving a police vehicle and a Volkswagen Passat on the A66 in South Bank,” a Cleveland police spokesperson said. “Sadly, the collision has resulted in multiple fatalities. There are significant emergency vehicles on the scene and the road will remain closed for some time.” The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which is investigating the crash, said officers from Cleveland force had spotted a suspicious vehicle. A pursuit began and the car travelled on to the A66 where it collided with a police car at 3.39am. The watchdog said investigators had been sent to review evidence, and that they were working with police to establish the circumstances of the collision. The investigation was opened on Saturday after a mandatory referral from the Cleveland force. North East ambulance service said it had been called to a two-vehicle crash and sent 14 units to the scene including ambulance crews, a specialist paramedic, a hazardous area response team and a doctor from Great North air ambulance service. A spokesperson said: “Sadly, despite the best efforts of everyone attending, a number of patients died at the scene. “We send condolences to all of those affected by such a tragic event and thank everyone for all they did to help.” Police have yet to confirm the number of fatalities. Anna Turley, MP for the Redcar constituency where the crash happened, said: “I am deeply saddened to hear of the fatal collision on the A66 this morning. “My thoughts are with the families and loved ones of those who have lost their lives, and with everyone affected by this terrible incident. “Thank you to all of our emergency services, who have worked through the night responding to this devastating incident. “We would ask everyone to avoid speculating online to respect the families and the police while they do their work at this terrible time.” Police said they were working to identify the victims and contact their families, and that the incident was “quickly evolving”. The A66 remains closed in both directions between Normanby Road and Church Lane in Eston. Photograph: Teodor Lazarev/Alamy Medical research Warning signs could predict inflammatory bowel disease a decade before diagnosis Antibody patterns in the blood may help doctors identify people at risk so they can be treated earlier, research shows Hanad Ahmed Sun 18 Oct 2026 18.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Patterns of antibodies in people’s blood could predict the onset of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) a decade before diagnosis, according to research that raises hopes for catching the condition early. Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, the two main forms of IBD, are typically treated only after symptoms appear, when the gut has already been damaged. But scientists found that the immune system sends warning signals up to a decade before diagnosis, paving the way for potentially earlier detection and even prevention. “For too long we have only been able to treat inflammatory bowel disease once the damage is done, and for many people that is too late,” said Dr Arno Bourgonje at the University Medical Centre Groningen in the Netherlands and the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York. “What we have shown is that the disease begins years before symptoms appear, and the immune system leaves warning signs long before diagnosis,” Bourgonje added. “This is not yet a test that can tell someone they will become ill, but it is an important step towards catching the disease earlier and, one day, preventing it.” At least 3.8 million people worldwide live with IBD, an immune condition that drives chronic inflammation of the digestive tract, causing pain, diarrhoea and fatigue. The exact cause is unknown, but a misfiring immune system, genetics and microbes living in the gut can all contribute. Treatment relies on anti-inflammatory and immune-suppressing drugs, but many patients do not respond, and a significant number go on to have surgery to remove damaged sections of bowel. Longstanding inflammation also raises the risk of bowel cancer. This has prompted scientists to look for the earlier signs of disease, in the hope of identifying people at risk before damage begins. Bourgonje and colleagues at Mount Sinai and the Medical University of Vienna ran tests on blood samples taken from US military personnel. They examined 2,000 samples from 500 people, 200 of whom later developed Crohn’s disease, and 200 who went on to develop ulcerative colitis. The remaining 100 developed neither condition. The blood samples were screened for antibodies that the immune system might have churned out in response to hundreds of thousands of fragments of proteins from bacteria, viruses, food and even the body’s own tissues. In people who went on to develop Crohn’s disease, antibodies against Epstein-Barr virus, which causes glandular fever, were more common, and the differences were already visible a decade before diagnosis. The signal was strongest in those who later developed more severe, complicated disease, which can narrow the bowel or create abnormal channels. People who developed ulcerative colitis showed a different pattern, including antibodies against one of the body’s own proteins. The findings, published in the journal Gut and presented at the United European Gastroenterology meeting in Barcelona, need to be confirmed in other groups of people, and the results show a link rather than proving the infections cause IBD. But the hope is that IBD could eventually follow the path of type 1 diabetes, where a blood test can identify people whose immune systems have begun attacking the pancreas before any symptoms appear, allowing treatment that delays the onset of disease. James Lindsay, a professor of gastroenterology at Barts Health , who was not involved in the research, said the study provided “important insights into the causes of Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, potentially adding new tools to help identify those at risk of IBD”. But he cautioned that the techniques were “very much a research tool” and not yet ready for the clinic. Marianne Radcliffe, the chief executive of Crohn’s & Colitis UK, a national patient charity, said: “For people affected by Crohn’s and colitis, research like this is an important step forward. Every new insight helps build a clearer understanding of how these conditions develop, including the changes that may occur years before symptoms appear.” Explore more on these topics Medical research Health Digestive disorders news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Brendan Nugent’s family say Haines has been their friend for more than 20 years Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Nino Bucci Tue 20 Oct 2026 05.18 EDT First published on Tue 20 Oct 2026 04.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Helen Haines’ alleged attacker, Brendan Nugent, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official. He will be held overnight to appear at Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday, Victoria police confirmed in a statement, adding that it would be alleged the attack was targeted. Victoria police arrested the 43-year-old Tarrawingee man on Monday afternoon after he allegedly struck the independent MP for Indi with a Toyota LandCruiser outside her electorate office in Wangaratta in northern Victoria . Haines remains in a critical but stable condition after being airlifted to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital for emergency surgery. She has lost one leg and surgeons were fighting on Tuesday to save the other leg. Police also said in the statement released late on Tuesday that one of its highway patrol officers responded to the incident only eight seconds after emergency services were called.
